newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr battered vs yen by Tokyo noon, down two yen.
newsitem.headline: Dlr battered vs yen by Tokyo noon, down two yen.

text.p: 0300 GMT TRADED HI/LO AS OF 0300 GMT
The dollar lost ground against the yen by midday Tokyo on Tuesday and briefly fell as much as about two yen from the previous New York closing level.

Expectations the interest rate gap between Japan and the U.S. will shrink, and U.S. worry about a rise in Japan's trade surplus triggered a slew of stop-loss sales to send the dollar down as low as 113.60 yen, its lowest since December 1996.
"Sentiment was completely destroyed, with no major supportive factors for the dollar in sight right now," said a trader at a European bank in Tokyo.
Interbank traders and overseas operators rushed to sell dollars and marks in favour of the yen, dealers said.

NHK television reported early Tuesday that Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party will make a recommendation to Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto by the end of this month that Japan raise its official discount rate. Meanwhile, speculation emerged that the U.S. Federal Reserve may leave its interest rates unchanged at its policy-setting meeting later in the day.
"Although there is uncertainty over changes in U.S. and Japanese interest rates, traders took everything as excuses to dump dollars," said a trust bank dealer.

On Monday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin warned against a sustained increase in Japan's current account surplus. "The question is will there be a sustained increase in the current account surplus?" Rubin said in response to reporters' questions following a speech to the Japan Society. "And if so I think that is a very serious problem," he said.
Japan's overall customs-cleared trade surplus grew 163.7 percent to 831.48 billion yen in April.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference on Tuesday that the rise in Japan's trade surplus is temporary and it is unlikely to become a major issue with other nations.
He added that the Group of Seven (G7) agreement on foreign exchange rates was filtering through to the markets.

The dollar's relentless fall forced some operators to sell dollars to limit their losses, partly in connection with their options positions, accelerating its tumble. Further stops are expected at 113.50 yen, dealers said.

"Stop-loss sales may emerge at every 0.50 yen fall all the way down to 110 yen," said a senior Japanese bank dealer. Many dealers said the dollar's recovery could be limited even if the Federal Reserve tightens credit because a perception that there will be no further rises in U.S. interest rates may grow.
The trust bank dealer said there would be psychological support at 110 yen, given recent remarks by major Japanese companies that an exchange rate of 110-120 yen is appropriate.
But others said there would be no guarantee that the dollar will stop falling there, because Japanese exporters and investors have failed to sell an adequate amount of dollars.
